    #Tutorial 1 (Atmosphere, Altitude, & Flight Speed)

    #Question 1

    P=ρRT

    ρ=287.058(223.26)26500​=0.41349 kg/m3

    From the ISA table, at P=26500 N/m2, pressure altitude hG​=10 km.

    From the ISA table, at T=223.26 K, temperature altitude hG​=10 km.

    From the ISA table, at ρ=0.41349 kg/m3, density altitude hG​=10 km.

    On a standard day, the pressure, temperature and density altitudes are the same.
    Aircraft performance will be as expected on a standard day at an altitude of 10 km.

    #Question 2

    P=ρRT

    ρ=287.058(249.2)26500​=0.37045 kg/m3

    From the ISA table, at P=26500 N/m2, pressure altitude hG​=10 km.

    From the ISA table, at T=249.2 K, temperature altitude hG​=6 km.

    From the ISA table, at ρ=0.37045 kg/m3, density altitude hG​=10.879 km.

    At ρ=0.36946 kg/m3, hG​=10.9 km.

    At ρ=0.37417 kg/m3, hG​=10.8 km.

    10.9−10.8hG​−10.8​=0.36946−0.374170.37045−0.37417​

    hG​=10.879 km

    The aircraft is flying at a pressure altitude of 10 km.

    Since temperature altitude of 6 km<10 km, it will be as though the aircraft is flying at a lower altitude, thus the day is hot. Since density altitude of 10.879 km>10 km, it will be as though the aircraft is flying at a higher altitude. Aircraft performance will be worse than that of a standard day due to the lower density, and thus decreased lift and thrust.

    #Question 3

    P=ρRT

    ρ=287.058(283)70121​=0.86316 kg/m3

    From the ISA table, at P=70121 N/m2, pressure altitude hG​=3 km.

    From the ISA table, at ρ=0.86316 kg/m3, density altitude hG​=3.5027 km.

    At ρ=0.85445 kg/m3, hG​=3.6 km.

    At ρ=0.86341 kg/m3, hG​=3.5 km.

    3.6−3.5hG​−3.5​=0.85445−0.863410.86316−0.86341​

    hG​=3.5027 km

    The aircraft’s takeoff is at a pressure altitude of 3 km.

    Since density altitude of 3.5027 km>3 km, it would be as though the aircraft is taking off at a higher altitude. Thus, density is lower, and aircraft performance will be worse than that of a standard day. Less thrust and lift will be generated, and a longer ground run will be required before takeoff.

    #Question 6

    Let Vh​ be the horizontal component of flight speed.
    Let Vv​ be the vertical component of flight speed.

    No Wind Condition

    Vh​=500cos30°=433.01 km/h

    Vv​=500sin30°=250 km/h

    With Headwind Condition

    Vh​ is affected by the headwind.
    Vv​ remains unchanged.

    tanθ=Vh(new)​Vv​​=500cos30°−50250​

    θ=tan−1500cos°−50250​

    θ=33.133°

    #Question 7

    Ground Speed=500 km/h

    Aircraft requires a ground speed of 500km/h (upwards).

    Resolving the windspeed into x and y,

    Wind=36cos45°=25.456 km/h (upwards)

    Wind=36sin45°=25.456 km/h (to the right)

    Velocity of aircraft in the upwards direction,

    Ground Speed=Airspeed+Wind

    500=Airspeed+25.456

    Airspeed=474.54 km/h (upwards)

    Since the wind has a velocity component to the right, the aircraft requires
    a velocity component to the left to cancel out the effects of the wind.

    Velocity of aircraft to the left,

    Airspeed=25.456 km/h (to the left)

    Airspeed of the aircraft,

    Airspeed=474.542+25.4562​

    Airspeed=475.23 km/h

    tanθ=474.5425.456​

    θ=3.0706°

    True Heading=360°−3.0706°

    True Heading=356.9°

    #Tutorial 5 (Climb Performance)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Maximum level flight speed of the aircraft is attained when the engines
    are producing the maximum thrust. Thus, thrust available is equal to
    the drag of the aircraft at this speed. Maximum power available can
    then be determined using P=TV=DV.

    Lift coefficient at maximum flight speed,

    L=21​ρVmax​2SCL​

    CL​=ρVmax​2S2L​

    CL​=1.225(2692)(45)2(9.81)(16330)​

    CL​=0.080322

    D=21​ρVmax​2SCD​

    Maximum power available,

    PA​=TVmax​=DVmax​

    PA​=28566(269)

    t=∫0h​R/C1​ dh

    15(60)=∫011000​ R(14000−h)14000​ dh

    900=R14000​∫011000​ 14000−h1​ dh

    1409R​=[−ln(14000−h)]011000​

    R=23.962 m/s

    #Part (a)

    Constraints of a level turn maneuver:

    • Aerodynamic capability — constrained by maximum CL​ achievable by the wings
    • Propulsive capability — constrained by maximum thrust that can be generated
    • Structural capability — constrained by maximum load the structure can carry

    From the V-n diagram, corner point occurs at the intersection of the stall boundary and the limit load factor. Thus, at this point, lift coefficient is CLmax​​, and lift required

    #Question 4

    To minimize the ground run distance, maximize F=T−D−μr​(W−L).

    Let q=21​ρV2S.

    F=T−qCD0​​−qkCL​2−μr​W+μr​qCL​

    Note that thrust, profile drag, and weight are constants.

    Differentiating with respect to CL​ and equating to zero,

    dCL​dF​=−2qkCL​+μr​q

    0=−2qkCL​+μr​q

    2kCL​=μr​

    CL​=2kμr​​

    Components of ground speed assuming no wind.

    #Apparent Approach Angle

    Due to the headwind, horizontal component of Va​ will be lower.

    Aircraft is flying with a horizontal airspeed of 65.133 m/s. A headwind reduces the horizontal ground speed of the aircraft (relative to the ground). However, airspeed
    of the aircraft still remains at 65.133 m/s (relative to the air).

    Va,hori​=Va​cos3°−Vhw​

    Va,hori​=65.133−10.29

    #Angle of Attack

    Required lift coefficient to maintain flight,

    CL​=1.4142

    Note that the velocity used is the airspeed along the flight path.

    3°×180π​=1.41420.157​−325218T​

    T=19076 N

    Note that the equation is derived using small angle approximation.
    Thus, the approach angle must be expressed in radians.
